content: Dengue is caused by viruses that are transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. Symptoms of dengue typically begin a few days after being bitten, but in some cases, they may take up to two weeks to appear. The clinical presentation of dengue can range from mild to severe. Common symptoms include fever accompanied by nausea, vomiting, a rash, headache, pain behind the eyes, and joint and muscle pain. In severe cases, dengue can lead to life-threatening complications such as shock, internal bleeding, and even death. It is important to note that not all individuals infected with the dengue virus will develop symptoms; only about 25% of infected individuals experience illness. Those who have been previously infected with dengue are at a higher risk of developing severe forms of the disease. Additionally, infants and pregnant women are more susceptible to severe dengue. Mosquitoes that transmit dengue are most active during the daytime, although they may bite less frequently at night. These mosquitoes are predominantly found in tropical and subtropical regions, including parts of the Americas, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and the Pacific Islands. Travelers to these areas are at an increased risk of contracting dengue, particularly if they spend significant time outdoors or visit during seasons when mosquito populations are more prevalent, such as during warm weather. 1. Use EPA-registered insect repellents: Apply insect repellents containing active ingredients such as picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), or para-menthane-diol (PMD). These repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women. If using sunscreen, apply the insect repellent after applying sunscreen. 2. Special precautions for children: Dress children in clothing that covers their arms and legs. Cover strollers and baby carriers with mosquito netting. When applying insect repellent to children, follow these guidelines: Avoid products containing OLE or PMD for children under 3 years old. Do not apply repellent to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, or broken/irritated skin. Adults should spray repellent onto their hands first and then apply it to the child’s face. 3. Wear protective clothing: 4. Treat clothing and gear with permethrin: Use 0.5% permethrin to treat clothing, footwear, and camping gear, or purchase pre-treated items. Permethrin-treated clothing remains effective after multiple washes, but follow product instructions for proper use and duration of protection. Do not apply permethrin directly to the skin. 5. Choose lodging with air conditioning or window and door screens to prevent mosquito entry. If staying in unscreened accommodations or sleeping outdoors, use a mosquito net. 6. Use mosquito nets: Sleep under a mosquito net, especially in areas where screened rooms are unavailable. Select a net that is compact, white, rectangular, and has 156 holes per square inch. Permethrin-treated mosquito nets offer enhanced protection. Follow label instructions to determine if the net can be washed. If bitten by mosquitoes, avoid scratching the bites to prevent secondary infections. Over-the-counter anti-itch creams or antihistamines can be applied to alleviate itching. Currently, there are no vaccines recommended for travelers to prevent dengue.
